obs: WHITING v. the Bank of the United States

“a decree of sale of mortgaged premises, was a final decree in the sense of the Act of Congress… This decision must have been made upon the general ground, that a decree, final upon the merits of the controversy between the parties… [and] the ulterior proceedings are but a mode of executing the original decree, like the award of an execution at law.”
“Certainly it is not a final judgment or order. For it does not put an end to the suit in the Orphans' Court…”

"the rule is well settled and of long standing that a judgment or decree to be final, within the meaning of that term as used in the acts of Congress giving this court jurisdiction on appeals or writs of error, must terminate the litigation between the parties on the merits of the case, so that if there should be an affirmance here, the court below would have nothing to do but to execute the judgment or decree which had been rendered."
"But here there has been no judgment in the suit, and therefore this section does not apply... No case can be brought up under 693, until there has been a final judgment or decree in the suit."
“Certainly it is not a final judgment or order. For it does not put an end to the suit in the Orphans' Court…”
United States v. California Coperative Canneries

"Thus, Congress limited the right of review to an appeal from the decree which disposed of all matters, ... and it precluded the possibility of an appeal to either court from an interlocutory decree."
"It was an order of the court, and one which finally disposed of all the issues in the case, leaving nothing to be done but the ministerial act of entering judgment in the trial court."
Federal Trade Commission v. Minneapolis-Honeywell Regulator Co.

"It is a principle reflected in the statutes which limit our appellate jurisdiction to those cases where review is sought within a prescribed period. Those statutes are not to be applied so as to permit a tolling of their time limitations because some event occurred in the lower court after judgment was rendered which is of no import to the matters to be dealt with on review."
Local No. 438 Construction & General Laborers' Union v. Curry
“the Court applied the salutary and long-standing rule that decisions upon interlocutory injunctions are not final judgments.”

“We held that the temporary injunction should be deemed a final judgment ‘particularly when postponing review would seriously erode the national labor policy …,’ and said further, ‘… authorizing the issuance of a temporary injunction … may effectively dispose of petitioner’s rights and render entirely illusory his right to review here …’”
